title: Checking if others already solved this sampling idea
summary: Prior-art and source-code audit for the claim that reservoir sampling's eviction randomness is unnecessary. VERDICT: GO-WITH-RESCOPE. (Q1) Draper & Saad SODA 2026 (arXiv:2505.18879v5) is a PARTIAL_SCOOP, not a kill: the word 'reservoir' appears 0 times in 476k characters, and their Eq. 1.7/Remark 1.3 make clear they optimise HOW a chosen distribution is realised, not WHICH distributions must be realised -- but their Remark 1.4/Corollary 1.7 DO cover the reservoir's state-dependent sequence, so they must be cited as the realisation layer. Bhattacharya et al. (arXiv:1407.1689) settle k=1 in the eps-error model at Theta(log(n/eps)) and prove bounded-bit exactness impossible; Breitner's comment thread settles exact k=1; Bodini & Durand (GASCom 2026) settle the OFFLINE k-subset case at log2 C(n,k)+O(k). k>=2 streaming is OPEN. (Q2) The balanced fiber map is textbook (normalized matching / de Bruijn SCD) -- claim the application only; exact deterministic balance is IMPOSSIBLE unless k | (i-k+1); and the per-step min-entropy coupling has NO polynomial special-case theorem (Kovacevic Thm 3.8 keeps row-sparse MEC strongly NP-hard). (Q3) The folklore claim is REFUTED: 0 of 15 quotations from 12 sources assert necessity (10 sufficiency-only, 5 descriptive) -- delete the 'overturns a textbook false belief' contribution. Ships a 16-row deployed-implementation table with verbatim eviction lines, RNG granularity and test-suite grades; 6 real bug reports including Apache DataSketches #647, an OPEN joint-distribution-only defect that per-item tests cannot detect. Own deterministic arithmetic (bit_accounting.py) refutes alternate hypothesis #4 for k>=10: the eviction term is 18-34% of total variate entropy at k=10 and 34-59% at k=100, so recycling alone does not subsume the coupling claim -- but the claimed '25-61%' holds only for 10<=k<=100, and the every-prefix constraint costs ~8x more than the final answer's own entropy.
answer:
**Bottom line: GO-WITH-RESCOPE.** The random-bit question for *exact,
every-prefix-uniform, k>=2* reservoir sampling is genuinely open, and the one
serious threat -- Draper & Saad's randomness recycling (SODA 2026) -- is a
PARTIAL_SCOOP that leaves the headline alive while becoming a mandatory
citation. But three of the hypothesis's supporting claims do not survive
contact with the primary sources, and one of them ("every textbook says uniform
eviction is necessary") must be deleted outright.

**Q1. Is the bit question open? Yes -- and Draper & Saad are the tool, not the
result.** Their model covers a sequence of distributions P_1, P_2, ... "subject
to any stochastic process", and Eq. 1.7 makes the scope precise: "P_i cannot
depend on fresh coins to be consumed by the sampler in future rounds, and that
it cannot depend on the internal history of the sampler other than through its
generated outputs X_{<i}" [2]. A reservoir's state *is* a deterministic function
of its own past outputs, so Remark 1.4 and Corollary 1.7 apply to reservoir
sampling directly -- their machinery would drive Algorithm R's cost to
H[X_1,...,X_n] + eps*n + W [2]. What it does **not** do is decide *which*
distributions the algorithm should realise. Remark 1.3 says so explicitly: "it
is essential to consider the surprisals and entropies of the random
distributions (P_1,...,P_n), and not the joint entropy H[X_1,...,X_n] of the
output sequence" [2]. The word "reservoir" appears **zero times** in the 476k
characters of the v5 HTML, "streaming"/"unknown length" zero times, and the
only k-subset-adjacent application is the Fisher-Yates shuffle [1, 2]; the
authors' C library README likewise never mentions reservoir, subset,
without-replacement or shuffle [3]. Verdict: **PARTIAL_SCOOP**. The paper must
cite them as the realisation layer and claim only the coupling/eviction novelty.

This also settles the fight with alternate hypothesis #4 ("the waste is in the
variates, not the coupling"). Our own arithmetic (`bit_accounting.py`,
deterministic, no RNG) sums the Shannon entropy of the variates Algorithm R
*chooses* to draw: the accept coin H_b(k/i) plus log2(k) per acceptance. The
eviction term's share of the total is 6-8% at k=2, 11-22% at k=4, 18-34% at
k=10, 27-48% at k=32, 34-59% at k=100 and 47-78% at k=1000 (over n = 1e4..1e9).
So recycling applied to classical Algorithm R recovers the *representational*
waste but leaves the eviction term entirely intact -- the coupling argument is
not subsumed. Two honest caveats fall out of the same table. First, the
hypothesis's headline band of "25-61%" is only attained for moderate-to-large k;
at k=2-4 the achievable saving is a fifth of that, and the paper must state the
(k, n) regime. Second, even the deterministic-eviction ideal is far above the
entropy of the final answer: at k=10, n=1e6 it costs ~1494 bits versus
log2 C(n,k) = 177.5 bits. The every-prefix constraint, not the eviction rule, is
the dominant cost -- a framing the paper should adopt rather than hide.

Two further prior-art findings matter. Bhattacharya, Issac, Jaiswal & Kumar
prove Theta(log(n/eps)) random bits for *epsilon-error* streaming sampling and,
critically, prove exactness is unattainable with bounded bits at all: "assume
that a uniform sample can be generated using r random bits ... This means that
2^r is divisible by n. This is a contradiction since n is a prime number" [4].
They also state "the lower bound on the number of random bits remains the same
if the sampling algorithm is allowed to store more than one item from the
stream" [4] -- but their sample size is 1 throughout; storing k items to output
1 is not sampling a k-subset, so the k>=2 *output* case is untouched.
ADJACENT, not a scoop. Second, Bodini & Durand solve the **offline** k-subset
problem entropically: "the expected net bit consumption (bits consumed minus
bits recycled) is log2 C(n,k) + O(k)" in O(n) time [10], building on the
random-bit model of Lumbroso [12] and the same group's set-partition work [11]. That is the offline
analogue of our target and must be cited; it makes the streaming/unknown-n
version the actual open cell. Fourteen further scoop-hunt queries (logged in
`research_report.md`) returned nothing combining random bits with k>=2 streaming
sampling. Attribution corrections: Algorithms X, Y, Z are all
Vitter 1985 TOMS (no 1987 paper); Vitter 1984 CACM holds A-D for known N [6, 8];
Li 1994 holds Algorithm L [9]; and the k=1 closed form is due to the comment
thread on Breitner's post, not to Breitner, who left it open [5].

**Q2. The mathematics is known in spirit, and one claim is outright wrong.**
The Boolean lattice's normalized matching property is textbook -- "It is easy to
show that 2^[n] is a rank-symmetric, unimodal normalized matching poset" [13] --
and de Bruijn/Tengbergen/Kruyswijk symmetric chain decompositions come with
three explicit constructions including the parenthesis-matching rule [14]. Claim
the *application*, not the object. Two corrections. (a) An **exactly** balanced
deterministic deletion map cannot exist in general: each (k-1)-subset of [i]
must receive C(i,k)/C(i,k-1) = (i-k+1)/k preimages, an integer only when
k | (i-k+1), so residual randomness is forced at most steps. Wagon & Wilf give
the sharp criterion for the natural sum-mod-k variant -- uniform iff for every
divisor d>1 of m, t mod d > n mod d -- which fails for most (n,t) [15]. (b) The claim that
the per-step minimum-entropy coupling is "small and exactly solvable" has **no
citable theorem behind it**. MEC is NP-hard (Kovacevic et al., Subset-Sum
reduction) and stays strongly NP-hard under row-sparsity: their Theorem 3.8
reduces 3-Partition to a coupling "having exactly one nonzero entry in every
row" [16]. All polynomial results are additive approximations -- 1 bit
(Cicalese et al. [17]), 0.53/1.22 bits (Compton et al. [18]), and a PTAS
polynomial only for constant m and eps [19]. ARIMEC's conditional guarantee
does not apply here [20], and the forest-support structure of optimal couplings
leaves C(mn, m+n-1) candidates [21]. Verdict: BRUTE_FORCE_ONLY, leaning
UNRESOLVED for our specific uniform-marginal Johnson-graph support.

**Q3. The folklore claim is not evidenced -- delete it.** Across 15 verbatim
quotations from 12 sources (Wikipedia, Vitter 1985, Stanford CS168, Weizmann,
Utah, Cornell, cs.stackexchange, StackOverflow, and four blog expositions),
**bucket A (strict necessity) = 0**, bucket B (sufficiency only) = 10, bucket C
(descriptive) = 5. Vitter writes "The candidate it replaces is chosen randomly
from the n candidates" and then "It is easy to see that the resulting set of n
candidates forms a random sample" [7] -- description plus sufficiency, never
necessity. Wikipedia's proof ends "By induction, Algorithm R produces a uniform
random sample of the inputs" [22]. Nobody claims an alternative fails -- not Stanford CS168 [29], Weizmann [24],
Utah [30], Cornell [26], cs.stackexchange [23], StackOverflow [31], nor the
blog expositions [25, 27, 28, 32]. The
"overturns a textbook false belief" contribution must be replaced by the true,
still-interesting statement: *uniform eviction is universally taught and
universally deployed, proofs are sufficiency-only, and the necessity question is
simply never asked.*

The 16-row source audit supports that softer claim strongly. Every deployed
*streaming* sampler evicts uniformly: Spark `(rand.nextDouble() * l).toLong`
[33], rust-random `rng.random_range(..i + 1 + amount)` [39], ClickHouse
`genRandom(total_values)` with visible `% limit` modulo bias [35], go-metrics
`rand.Int63n(s.count)` [48], gstamatelat `sample.set(random.nextInt(sampleSize),
item)` [40], sklearn `j = rng_randint(0, i + 1)` [43]. The priority-queue family
(Flink, Beam, DuckDB) spends a full float64 per element instead [45, 44, 37]. Non-streaming contrast rows -- NumPy [42], Redis [50],
PostgreSQL [51], TensorFlow's shuffle buffer [49] -- and Guava, which ships no
reservoir sampler at all [46], bound how far the folklore reaches.
Algorithm-L skip code uses naive `Math.log(1 - W)` [40] and `log(r) / log(t_w)`
[37], never log1p/expm1 -- direct support for alternate hypothesis #2. Spark's
`GapSampling` is the lone `math.log1p(-f)` user [33].

**Alternate hypothesis #1 needs rescoping, not killing.** It is *not* true that
test suites only check first-order statistics: CPython asserts every ordered
permutation appears [41], sklearn asserts every C(n,k) frozenset appears [43],
commons-rng runs a chi-square over all 10 2-subsets [47]. But all three are
offline samplers on tiny n. Every *streaming* sampler audited is
first-order-only or has no distributional test at all [33, 35, 37, 39, 40, 48].
And there is a real, unpatched joint-only defect in the wild: Apache
DataSketches #647 -- "for items 0 to k-1, they can only ever appear at that
specific index" -- correct marginals, wrong joint [53]. Meanwhile Spark's own
reviewer wrote "the test suite never actually tests for correctness, just basic
input/output sizes" [34], and four of five confirmed fixed bugs (TiKV, Spark,
DuckDB, dataprof) were first-order and none was caught by existing tests
[52, 34, 38, 54]; the sixth confirmed bug, a ClickHouse self-merge aliasing
fault, was likewise found by an automated reviewer, not by tests [36].

**Ranked re-assessment.** (1) Main hypothesis, rescoped to "bit cost of exact
every-prefix-uniform k>=2 sampling, with Draper-Saad as the realisation layer" --
GO. (2) Alternate #1, rescoped to *streaming* samplers, with DataSketches #647
as a real-world target -- GO, strong. (3) Alternate #2 (Algorithm-L float
defect) -- GO, evidence gathered. (4) Alternate #4 -- REFUTED by the arithmetic
above for k >= 10.

scoop_verdicts.work: Draper & Saad, Efficient Online Random Sampling via Randomness Recycling
scoop_verdicts.citation: Thomas L. Draper, Feras A. Saad. Proc. 2026 ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA), pp. 2473-2511, SIAM 2026. doi:10.1137/1.9781611978971.89
scoop_verdicts.version_and_access_date: arXiv:2505.18879v5 (submitted 24 May 2025, last revised 7 May 2026); accessed 2026-09-18
scoop_verdicts.deciding_quote: cannot depend on fresh coins to be consumed by the sampler in future rounds, and that it cannot depend on the internal history of the sampler other than through its generated outputs
scoop_verdicts.section: Section 1.1 (Problem Statement), Eq. 1.7; with Remark 1.3, Remark 1.4, Theorem 1.5, Corollary 1.7
scoop_verdicts.what_it_covers: An online sampler that realises ANY sequence of rational discrete distributions -- including sequences where each P_i is a deterministic function of the algorithm's own previous outputs (Remark 1.4) -- within eps bits of the Shannon bound using O(log(1/eps)) space. Because a reservoir's state is a function of its own past accept/evict outputs, their Corollary 1.7 applies to reservoir sampling and would give cost < H[X_1,...,X_n] + eps*n + W_{d,eps}.
scoop_verdicts.what_it_does_not_cover: Which distribution sequence the algorithm ought to realise. Remark 1.3 explicitly separates sum_i H(P_i) from H[X_1,...,X_n] and warns the former is the right quantity. The string 'reservoir' occurs 0 times in the 476,303-character v5 HTML; 'streaming', 'data stream' and 'unknown length' occur 0 times; 'without replacement' occurs only inside the abstract's generic phrasing; the only subset-adjacent application is the Fisher-Yates shuffle. The accompanying C library's README lists inversion, lookup-table, alias, FLDR and ALDR samplers and never mentions reservoir, subset, without-replacement or shuffle.
scoop_verdicts.implication_for_our_claim: HEADLINE SURVIVES, but the paper must (a) cite Draper-Saad as the realisation layer that makes any chosen variate sequence cost its own entropy, and (b) claim novelty only for the coupling question -- which eviction distribution must be realised at all. Our own arithmetic shows recycling on classical Algorithm R still pays the full k*log2(k)*(H_n - H_k) eviction term, which is 18-34% of the total at k=10 and 34-59% at k=100, so alternate hypothesis #4 ('the waste is only representational') is refuted for k >= 10.

scoop_verdicts.work: Bhattacharya, Issac, Jaiswal & Kumar, Sampling in Space Restricted Settings
scoop_verdicts.citation: Anup Bhattacharya, Davis Issac, Ragesh Jaiswal, Amit Kumar. arXiv:1407.1689v3 (16 Jan 2015); COCOON 2015; Algorithmica 80:1439-1458, 2018.
scoop_verdicts.deciding_quote: It is important to point out that the lower bound on the number of random bits remains the same if the sampling algorithm is allowed to store more than one item from the stream. Our sampling algorithm matches this lower bound while storing only one item from the stream.
scoop_verdicts.section: Section 1, 'Our contributions' / end of contributions paragraph
scoop_verdicts.what_it_covers: Exact Theta(log(n/eps)) random-bit upper and lower bounds for maintaining a SIZE-ONE uniform sample over a stream of unknown length, in the eps-error model where the sampler may output a null answer with probability <= eps. Also proves exact uniform sampling with a bounded number of bits is impossible: 'assume that a uniform sample can be generated using r random bits for some finite r ... This means that 2^r is divisible by n. This is a contradiction since n is a prime number.' Also records that classical reservoir sampling costs Omega(n log n) bits in expectation and (footnote 3) that 'a more advanced sampling technique by Vitter requires Omega((log n)^2) random bits in expectation'.
scoop_verdicts.what_it_does_not_cover: Sample size k >= 2. The quoted sentence concerns an algorithm that STORES more than one item while still OUTPUTTING a single uniform element; it is not a statement about sampling a uniform k-subset. No theorem, remark or open-problem sentence in the paper addresses k-subset output. The paper also never charges exact sampling a quadratically larger cost -- it charges exact sampling an UNBOUNDED worst-case cost (the primality argument) and works in the eps-error model instead.
scoop_verdicts.implication_for_our_claim: This is the closest existing bit-complexity result and must be the paper's baseline. It supplies (i) the impossibility of bounded-bit exactness, (ii) the k=1 lower bound, and (iii) the eps-error framing our exact model deliberately rejects. It leaves k >= 2 open. CORRECTION TO THE HYPOTHESIS: do not assert they 'charge exact sampling a quadratically larger cost'; what is quadratic is Vitter's variate-based method at (log n)^2, cited in their footnote 3.

scoop_verdicts.work: Breitner, Reservoir sampling with few random bits (blog post + comment thread)
scoop_verdicts.citation: Joachim Breitner, blog post #737, published 2018-03-25; comment #1 Benjamin Price 2018-04-18; comment #2 Christoph Pfister 2019-01-31.
scoop_verdicts.what_it_covers: The k=1 case in full: an interval/arithmetic-coding reservoir sampler; the exact entropy of the decision sequence; the asymptotic (ln n)^2/(2 ln 2); and the bound E[#coin flips] < H(X_2,...,X_n) + 3 for the blog's own procedure, versus the Knuth-Yao optimum of H + 2.
scoop_verdicts.what_it_does_not_cover: k >= 2. Nothing in the post or either comment mentions a reservoir of size greater than one. The post's own 'Open questions' section asks only whether the k=1 algorithm is optimal and what its expected coin count is.
scoop_verdicts.implication_for_our_claim: SAFE TO CITE as the k=1 precedent, but with two attribution corrections. (1) Breitner did NOT derive the closed form: he explicitly asks 'What is the expected number of coin throws for n prisoners?' and the formula, the +3 bound and the asymptotic all come from the comment thread -- Benjamin Price (2018-04-18) for the Theta((log n)^2) lower bound and Christoph Pfister (2019-01-31) for the closed form and the H+3 result. (2) Price's comment is the clearest existing statement of the paper's own core insight: 'The process described doesn't just choose one person, but chooses a sequence of people ... a better lower bound for the number of coin tosses is not the entropy of uniform selection from [n], but rather the entropy of selecting S subset [n].' Our bit_accounting.py reproduces the closed form to 6 decimals at n=1e3, 1e5 and 1e6, so the hypothesis's transcription of the formula is CORRECT.

scoop_verdicts.work: Bodini & Durand, Entropic Generation of Binary Words
scoop_verdicts.citation: Olivier Bodini, Francis Durand. GASCom 2026, EPTCS 445, 2026, pp. 38-46. doi:10.4204/EPTCS.445.6
scoop_verdicts.deciding_quote: The uniform generation of k Hamming weight binary words, equivalent to sampling k-subsets from n elements, relies on random bits, which can be expensive. We introduce a novel paradigm-random bit recycling-and use it to generate such binary words in linear time while consuming as few random bits as possible.
scoop_verdicts.section: Abstract; Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 in Sections 3-4
scoop_verdicts.what_it_covers: The OFFLINE k-subset problem in the random-bit model, solved essentially optimally: 'the expected net bit consumption (bits consumed minus bits recycled) is log2 C(n,k) + O(k)' in expected O(n) time, in the polynomially sparse regime k ~ n^beta. They explicitly note the concurrent existence of the recycling paradigm elsewhere, citing Draper-Saad '[5] for online sampling'.
scoop_verdicts.what_it_does_not_cover: Streaming with unknown n, and the every-prefix-uniform constraint. Their algorithm is an offline Fisher-Yates insertion plus permutation deconstruction; it needs n in advance and produces one word at the end, never maintaining a valid sample at every prefix.
scoop_verdicts.implication_for_our_claim: IMPORTANT AND PREVIOUSLY UNCITED. This is the offline analogue of our target and proves the k-subset random-bit question is an active research area, which strengthens the motivation but narrows the novelty claim to the streaming/every-prefix cell. It also gives the right comparison point: offline costs log2 C(n,k) + O(k); our arithmetic shows the every-prefix constraint costs roughly an order of magnitude more (1494 vs 177.5 bits at k=10, n=1e6). That gap -- the price of anytime-validity -- is arguably a better headline than the eviction saving.

scoop_verdicts.work: Vitter, Random Sampling with a Reservoir (Algorithms R, X, Y, Z)
scoop_verdicts.citation: Jeffrey Scott Vitter. ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 11(1):37-57, March 1985.
scoop_verdicts.deciding_quote: Table I. Performance of Algorithms R, X, Y, and Z -- Average number of uniform random variates: R: N-n; X: ~2n ln(N/n); Y: ~2n ln(N/n); Z: ~3n ln(N/n)

The eviction rule is stated as 'The candidate it replaces is chosen randomly from the n candidates', and the random source is 'The random number generator RANDOM returns a real number in the unit interval.'
scoop_verdicts.what_it_does_not_cover: Random bits. The word 'bit' does not appear as a cost metric anywhere in the performance analysis; Table I's column heading is literally 'Average number of uniform random variates'. The paper has no entropy accounting at all.
scoop_verdicts.implication_for_our_claim: CONFIRMS the paper's central framing that the classical literature counts variates, not bits. CORRECTION TO THE HYPOTHESIS: Algorithms X, Y and Z are all Vitter 1985 TOMS 11(1); there is no 1987 paper. Vitter 1984 (CACM 27(7):703-718, 'Faster methods for random sampling') contains Algorithms A, B, C and D for the KNOWN-N sequential sampling problem -- 'The main result of this paper is the design and analysis of Algorithm D' -- and is a different problem.

attribution_map.object: normalized matching property of the Boolean lattice (existence of a balanced fractional fiber map between consecutive levels)
attribution_map.canonical_citation: Istvan Tomon, 'Decompositions of the Boolean lattice into rank-symmetric chains', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 23(2) (2016) #P2.53 -- restating the classical fact; originally LYM / Kleitman.
attribution_map.quote: A bipartite graph G = (A, B, E) is a normalized matching graph, if for any X subset A we have |X|/|A| <= |Gamma(X)|/|B| ... It is easy to show that 2^[n] is a rank-symmetric, unimodal normalized matching poset.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: Nothing about the object. Cite it as textbook and claim only the streaming APPLICATION and the O(k) online evaluation rule. Presenting a 'balanced fiber map' as new would be an attribution error a combinatorics-literate reviewer catches on sight.

attribution_map.object: symmetric chain decomposition (SCD) of the Boolean lattice, with explicit constructions
attribution_map.canonical_citation: de Bruijn, Tengbergen & Kruyswijk (1951); later Kleitman; three explicit constructions (recursive, greedy lexicographic matching, parenthesis pairing) written out in Petr Gregor, 'Hypercube problems', Lecture 17, Charles University, 21 Dec 2017 (scribe O. Micka, updated 17 Jun 2018).
attribution_map.quote: We construct an SCD as follows. For every level k, 0 <= k <= n-1, we go through vertices on level k in lexicographical order (starting with the smallest one) and match them with their lexicographically smallest unmatched neighbor on level k+1.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: Nothing about the construction. Note that an SCD gives a MATCHING between consecutive levels, which is not what a reservoir step needs (a reservoir step needs a surjective, degree-balanced map, not an injection), so SCDs are related background rather than the tool.

attribution_map.object: exactly balanced deterministic element-deletion map from k-subsets of [i] onto (k-1)-subsets of [i]
attribution_map.status: NOT_FOUND -- and provably impossible in general
attribution_map.canonical_citation: Elementary counting, stated here; no source asserts existence. The level-k/level-(k-1) bipartite graph is biregular with degrees k and i-k+1.
attribution_map.quote: A graded poset P is a normalized matching poset (or satisfies the normalized matching property), if the bipartite comparability graph induced on any two levels A_i and A_j is a normalized matching graph for i, j in {0, ..., n}, i != j.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: A CORRECTION, not a claim. For a deterministic deletion rule to induce the uniform distribution on (k-1)-subsets, every (k-1)-subset must receive exactly C(i,k)/C(i,k-1) = (i-k+1)/k preimages, which is an integer only when k divides i-k+1. At most steps it does not, so some residual randomness is unavoidable and the paper must present a NEAR-deterministic rule with an explicit, quantified residue rather than an exactly balanced map. The normalized matching property guarantees only the FRACTIONAL (randomised) balanced map, which is exactly the classical Algorithm R.

attribution_map.object: 'sum of elements mod k' as a near-uniform statistic on random k-subsets
attribution_map.canonical_citation: Stan Wagon & Herbert S. Wilf, 'When are subset sums equidistributed modulo m?', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 1(1) (1994) #R3. doi:10.37236/1183
attribution_map.quote: We ask: for which triples (n,t,m) are the C(n,t) values of f(S) uniformly distributed in the residue classes mod m? The obvious necessary condition, that m divides C(n,t), is not sufficient, but a q-analogue of that condition is both necessary and sufficient ... We show that this condition is equivalent to: for each divisor d>1 of m, we have t mod d > n mod d.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: Nothing about the statistic; cite Wagon-Wilf. Critically, their theorem is a SHARP CHARACTERISATION of when the statistic is exactly uniform, and the condition 't mod d > n mod d' fails for most (n,t) pairs -- so a sum-mod-k construction is exactly balanced only on a thin set of steps. This independently confirms the divisibility obstruction above and gives a citable, computable criterion for exactly which steps are clean.

attribution_map.object: per-step minimum-entropy coupling, and the claim that it is 'small and exactly solvable'
attribution_map.status: NOT_FOUND (no supporting theorem); the general problem is KNOWN_IN_PRINT as NP-hard
attribution_map.canonical_citation: M. Kovacevic, I. Stanojevic, V. Senk, 'On the entropy of couplings', arXiv:1303.3235; Problems of Information Transmission, 2015.
attribution_map.quote: Theorem 3.8. Optimal channel is NP-hard. Proof. We prove the claim by reducing 3-Partition to Optimal channel. ... a partition with desired properties exists if and only if there is a matrix C in C(P,m) ... having exactly one nonzero entry in every row.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: Only that the per-step instance is SMALL ENOUGH TO BRUTE-FORCE at the k of interest, verified computationally -- not that it is polynomially solvable. Theorem 3.8 shows row-sparsity alone does not buy tractability (3-Partition reduction, so strongly NP-hard), and Theorem 3.4 shows hardness already at support size 2 on one marginal. Every polynomial guarantee in the literature is additive-approximate: 1 bit (Cicalese-Gargano-Vaccaro Thm 2), 0.53 bits for m=2 / 1.22 general (Compton et al.), and Compton's 2025 PTAS is polynomial only for CONSTANT m and eps. No paper addresses uniform marginals on a Johnson-graph deletion support.

attribution_map.object: exact solvability of the specific instance (uniform marginals, element-deletion sparse support)
attribution_map.canonical_citation: Searched across Kovacevic et al. 2015, Cicalese-Gargano-Vaccaro 2019, Compton et al. 2023, Compton 2025, Sokota et al. 2024 (ARIMEC), and arXiv:2505.12227 on extreme points of coupling polytopes.
attribution_map.quote: Computing the minimum-entropy coupling is NP-hard, but there has been significant progress in designing approximation algorithms; prior to this work, the best known polynomial-time algorithms attain guarantees of the form H(ALG) <= H(OPT) + c, where c is about 0.53 for m=2, and c is about 1.22 for general m.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: That the question is OPEN. A reviewer will accept 'we solve the per-step instance exactly by enumeration at the k we test, and leave its complexity open', and will reject 'the per-step problem is a known polynomial special case'. Settling it needs either a total-unimodularity/matroid-intersection argument for this family or a targeted hardness reduction -- neither exists.

attribution_map.object: randomness recycling as the realisation layer
attribution_map.canonical_citation: Draper & Saad, SODA 2026 (arXiv:2505.18879v5); independently and concurrently, Bodini & Durand, GASCom 2026 (EPTCS 445:38-46) for the offline k-subset case.
attribution_map.quote: Corollary 1.7. Let P := {p_i(.|X_1,...,X_{i-1})}_{i>=1} denote a sequence of conditional distributions for random variables X := (X_i)_{i>=1}, whose probabilities have common denominator d >= 1. For any eps>0, there exists an online random sampling algorithm that generates X whose entropy cost satisfies E[t_n(C,P)] < H[X_1,...,X_n] + eps*n + W_{d,eps}.
attribution_map.what_we_may_claim: Nothing. Use it, cite it, and make explicit that our contribution operates one level up -- choosing the conditional sequence whose joint entropy H[X_1,...,X_n] their corollary then pays.

bug_reports.summary: OPEN, UNPATCHED, and the single most valuable finding for alternate hypothesis #1: a maintainer-authored design note showing that the standard merge of two serialized reservoirs preserves correct per-item MARGINALS while corrupting the JOINT/positional distribution. Verbatim: 'You can almost use the first t and s-t samples from s1 and s2, respectively, except that there's a position bias from the initial reservoir fill. For items 0 to k-1, they can only ever appear at that specific index.' A per-item frequency test cannot detect this by construction. Self-identified in design discussion ('after discussing with a stats person about a year ago'), not by any test; three candidate fixes proposed, none merged (dated 2025-02-03).

SPARK-18678, 2016-12-03. Off-by-one in reservoirSampleAndCount made the replacement probability k/(l-1) instead of k/l, biasing small-k samples. Found by a committer auditing the code. The reviewer's own words are the strongest available evidence that the field does not test sampler correctness: 'Now that I'm looking at it, the test suite never actually tests for correctness, just basic input/output sizes.' Merged to master and backported to Spark 2.1.

'Reservoir Sampling is broken since DuckDB 1.2.0', reported 2025-06-30 by an external user who noticed q25/q50/q75 of a uniform population shifting across releases. Two compounding defects in the fast-to-slow mode switch: replacement keys were drawn uniformly between a precomputed minimum and 1 when the correct law is a Beta(n,1) order statistic, and next_index_to_sample used round instead of ceil. Fix quote: 'The main issue here is that the top k values among n uniform samples, known as order statistics, do not follow a uniform distribution, resulting in a skew.' This is exactly the floating-point/order-statistic failure mode alternate hypothesis #2 predicts for Algorithm-L-family code.

2026-07-17. RegionInfo::add_key_ranges sampled from 0..n instead of 0..=n, so with capacity 1 the second observation ALWAYS evicted the first. 'observation n is admitted with probability sample_num / n, while Algorithm R requires sample_num / (n + 1).' Found by manual code review; the fix PR (#19851) added unit test coverage that did not previously exist.

2026-08-31. StreamReservoirSampler::merge() pooled two reservoirs and subsampled uniformly, ignoring each side's population count: 'a 100-row partition merged into a 10,000-row one took about 52 of 100 sample slots instead of about 1.' Fixed by drawing survivors from the hypergeometric distribution. Found by self-audit; merge() had no production caller and no covering test.

2026-04-04, maintainer-labelled 'bug: Confirmed user-visible misbehaviour in official release'. ReservoirSamplerDeterministic::merge() lacks the 'if (this == &b) return;' self-merge guard that ReservoirSampler::merge() already has, so a state merged with itself iterates b.samples while insertImpl overwrites the same array. Reproduction returns 58415 instead of ~50467.5 on 100k rows. Found by an automated code-review bot scanning an unrelated PR, not by the test suite. Classified 'other' (memory aliasing, not a distributional bias).

settled_by_literature: MAIN HYPOTHESIS -- 'the random-bit cost of exact every-prefix-uniform k>=2 reservoir sampling is unstudied': NOT settled by prior art. The k=1 case is settled twice over (Bhattacharya et al. arXiv:1407.1689 for the eps-error model, Theta(log(n/eps)); Breitner's comment thread for the exact model, H = log2 n + sum (1/j)log2(j-1) ~ (ln n)^2/(2 ln 2)). The k>=2 case is not addressed anywhere found. OPEN.

MAIN HYPOTHESIS -- 'uniformly random eviction can be replaced by a (near-)deterministic rule without breaking every-prefix uniformity': NOT settled, but PARTLY CONSTRAINED. Exact determinism is impossible whenever k does not divide i-k+1 (elementary counting), and Wagon-Wilf (eljc 1994 #R3) gives the sharp criterion for when a sum-mod-k statistic is exactly uniform. The paper must claim a near-deterministic rule with quantified residue.

MAIN HYPOTHESIS -- 'the balanced fiber map is new': SETTLED AGAINST. The Boolean lattice's normalized matching property (Tomon eljc 23(2) #P2.53, restating the classical fact) already gives the fractional balanced map, and de Bruijn/Tengbergen/Kruyswijk SCDs give explicit level-to-level constructions (Gregor, Hypercube problems L17). Claim the streaming application only.

MAIN HYPOTHESIS -- 'the per-step minimum-entropy coupling is exactly solvable': NOT SUPPORTED by any citable theorem, and the nearest results point the other way. Kovacevic-Stanojevic-Senk Thm 3.4 (Subset-Sum) and Thm 3.8 (3-Partition, row-sparse) show hardness survives both small support and row sparsity. Claim brute-force-at-our-k and state the complexity as open.

ALTERNATE #1 -- 'the standard uniformity test is nearly blind to joint-distribution defects': PARTLY settled, and needs rescoping. FALSE as stated for offline samplers: CPython tests every ordered permutation, scikit-learn tests every C(n,k) frozenset, Apache Commons RNG runs a chi-square over all 2-subsets. TRUE for every streaming sampler audited (Spark, ClickHouse, DuckDB, rust-random, gstamatelat, go-metrics, Flink, Beam): first-order-only or no distributional test at all. A real unpatched joint-only defect exists (Apache DataSketches #647) and is the natural validation target.

ALTERNATE #2 -- 'Algorithm L implementations use numerically naive log(1-W)': CONFIRMED by source inspection, not settled by any paper. gstamatelat LiLSampling uses 'Math.log(random1) / Math.log(1 - W)'; DuckDB uses 'log(r) / log(t_w)'; neither repo contains log1p or expm1 anywhere in its sampling code. Spark's GapSampling is the only log1p user found, and it is not the reservoir path. DuckDB issue #18099 is a real, fixed order-statistics bug in exactly this code.

ALTERNATE #4 -- 'the waste is in the variates, not the coupling': REFUTED for k >= 10 by deterministic arithmetic in bit_accounting.py. Draper-Saad recycling drives realisation cost to sum_i H(P_i), but the eviction term k*log2(k)*(H_n - H_k) is 18-34% of that sum at k=10 and 34-59% at k=100 over n = 1e4..1e9. It is, however, a fair characterisation at k=2 (6-8%).

UNIVERSALLY MISSED BY THE HYPOTHESIS -- the every-prefix constraint, not the eviction rule, dominates. Even a perfectly deterministic-eviction sampler costs ~1494 bits at k=10, n=1e6 versus log2 C(n,k) = 177.5 bits for the final answer, and Bodini-Durand already achieve log2 C(n,k) + O(k) offline. The price of anytime-validity is a factor of ~8 and is arguably the better headline.
corrections_to_the_hypothesis: 'Every textbook, Wikipedia and StackOverflow states uniform eviction is necessary.' FALSE. Across 15 verbatim quotations from 12 distinct sources, bucket A (strict necessity asserted) = 0, bucket B (sufficiency only) = 10, bucket C (descriptive) = 5. Not one source claims a non-uniform eviction rule would bias the sample. DELETE the 'overturns a textbook false belief' contribution and replace with: 'uniform eviction is universally taught, universally deployed, and its necessity is never discussed -- every proof found is sufficiency-only.'

Vitter's Algorithms X, Y and Z are ALL in Vitter 1985, ACM TOMS 11(1):37-57, not split across 1985 and 1987. There is no 1987 Vitter reservoir paper. Vitter 1984, CACM 27(7):703-718 ('Faster methods for random sampling') contains Algorithms A, B, C and D for the known-N sequential sampling problem -- a different problem.

The k=1 entropy closed form H = log2(n) + sum_{k=2..n} (1/k) log2(k-1) ~ (ln n)^2/(2 ln 2) is CORRECTLY transcribed (reproduced to 6 decimals in bit_accounting.py at n=1e3, 1e5, 1e6), but it is NOT Breitner's result. Breitner's 2018-03-25 post explicitly asks 'What is the expected number of coin throws for n prisoners?' as an open question. The Theta((log n)^2) lower bound is comment #1 by Benjamin Price (2018-04-18) and the closed form, the H+2 Knuth-Yao optimum and the H+3 bound for Breitner's procedure are comment #2 by Christoph Pfister (2019-01-31). Cite the commenters.

Bhattacharya, Issac, Jaiswal & Kumar do NOT 'charge exact sampling a quadratically larger cost'. They show exact uniform sampling is IMPOSSIBLE with any bounded number of bits (primality argument) and therefore work in the eps-error model with a tight Theta(log(n/eps)). The quadratic figure in their paper is footnote 3's remark that Vitter's advanced method needs Omega((log n)^2) bits in expectation -- a different claim about a different algorithm.

The claimed 25-61% eviction saving is regime-dependent and overstated for small k. Computed eviction share of the total variate entropy: k=2 -> 5.9-11.5%; k=4 -> 11.5-22.1%; k=10 -> 18.4-34.4%; k=32 -> 26.5-47.9%; k=100 -> 33.8-59.3%; k=1000 -> 46.8-78.5% (ranges over n = 1e9 down to 1e4). The paper must state (k, n) explicitly; '25-61%' corresponds roughly to 10 <= k <= 100.

'The balanced fiber map is an exactly balanced deterministic deletion rule.' Impossible in general. Each (k-1)-subset of [i] must receive C(i,k)/C(i,k-1) = (i-k+1)/k preimages, an integer only when k | (i-k+1). Wagon & Wilf (1994) give the exact criterion for the sum-mod-k variant: uniformity holds iff for every divisor d>1 of m, t mod d > n mod d. Reframe as a near-deterministic rule with an explicit residual-randomness budget.

'The per-step min-entropy coupling is a known polynomial special case.' No such theorem exists. MEC is NP-hard even when one marginal has support 2 (Kovacevic et al. Thm 3.4) and strongly NP-hard under one-nonzero-per-row sparsity (Thm 3.8, 3-Partition). All polynomial results are additive approximations; Compton's 2025 PTAS is polynomial only for constant m and eps.

Draper & Saad's framework DOES cover the reservoir's state-dependent distribution sequence (Remark 1.4 / Corollary 1.7 / Eq. 1.7), contrary to a natural reading of the hypothesis that it handles only exogenous processes. The correct distinction is Remark 1.3's: they optimise HOW a chosen distribution is realised, not WHICH distributions must be realised. State this precisely or a reviewer who knows the paper will read the framing as a misrepresentation.

'Every implementation evicts uniformly at random.' True for the Algorithm-R/L family but not for all deployed k-of-stream samplers. Apache Flink, Apache Beam and DuckDB use bottom-k / A-Res priority queues that evict the minimum-key element deterministically, spending a full float per element on the key instead. Redis, PostgreSQL tsm_system_rows, NumPy, CPython and Apache Commons RNG are not streaming samplers at all. Guava ships no reservoir sampler.

The paper's implicit baseline should not be 'log2 C(n,k) is unattainable'. Bodini & Durand (GASCom 2026) attain log2 C(n,k) + O(k) in O(n) time for the OFFLINE k-subset problem. The correct statement is that the every-prefix constraint costs roughly an order of magnitude more than the offline optimum, and that gap has not been characterised.

follow_up_questions: What is the exact minimum of H(S_k, S_{k+1}, ..., S_n) over all couplings whose marginals are uniform on the k-subsets of every prefix -- is the accept-coin term sum_i H_b(k/i) actually a lower bound, or can a coupling that correlates the accept decision with the reservoir contents beat it? Our arithmetic assumes the accept coin is irreducible; nothing found proves it.

Is minimum-entropy coupling with uniform marginals on consecutive Johnson-graph levels (support = element deletion) polynomial-time solvable, or strongly NP-hard? Kovacevic et al. Thm 3.8 shows row-sparsity alone does not help, but the uniform-marginal, biregular, transitive-automorphism-group structure here is far more special than anything in that reduction.

Does Draper-Saad recycling applied on top of classical Algorithm R actually attain sum_i [H_b(k/i) + (k/i)log2 k] in practice, and at what value of eps and what auxiliary-state size? Their C library implements the recycling primitives but ships no reservoir example, so this needs to be built and measured before the paper can quote a real end-to-end saving.

Would a second-order (pairwise co-occurrence) test actually have caught Apache DataSketches #647 at realistic sample sizes, and what is its power relative to the first-order tests that Spark, Flink and gstamatelat ship? That is the concrete, falsifiable experiment alternate hypothesis #1 now has a real target for.
